result.what_it_is: A short beginner tutorial (Part 1 only, by Ayoub Ennaoui, published 2025-04-19) on streaming JSON over a FastAPI WebSocket to a future Angular page. The whole backend is one endpoint, /ws/odds, that sends RANDOM numbers for a placeholder "Team A vs Team B" every 3 seconds. It uses no odds API, no vendor, no scraper, no database and no real bookmaker data. Part 2 (the Angular client) is announced but I found no sign it was ever published. I read the full body text on 2026-10-07 from the author's public Medium RSS feed (https://medium.com/feed/@ayoubennaoui20, HTTP 200). The article page itself returned a Cloudflare challenge (403) and I did not work around it.
result.upstream_data_source: None. The "odds" are generated in the server loop with random.uniform(1.5, 2.5). The author says so: "To keep things simple and focused on WebSocket functionality, we simulate the odds data instead of calling an external API or accessing a database." The code has no HTTP client, no vendor key and no odds provider. load_dotenv() and os are imported but nothing reads an API key. No other upstream is named anywhere in the text.
result.push_or_poll: Server-to-browser PUSH over a WebSocket, but timer-driven rather than change-driven: a per-connection "while True" loop does send_json() then asyncio.sleep(3), whether or not anything changed. There is no upstream poll or push because there is no upstream. If a real feed were bolted on, a viewer would see that feed's age plus up to 3 s (INFERRED from the loop).
result.claimed_latency_or_refresh: Only prose and a code comment. Prose: "Every second matters — the odds are shifting based on goals, red cards, substitutions". Comment: "# simulate new odds every 3 seconds". The article states no latency number for any real feed because it uses none. It also says WebSockets "Reduce latency and bandwidth usage", a generic claim that says nothing about how fresh a price is.
result.measured_or_verified_age: None. The payload is {"match": ..., "odds": {"Team A": float, "Team B": float}} with no timestamp, no bookmaker and no market id. There is no real price, so it has no age. No third-party measurement exists, because the code is a demo.
result.coverage: None. One hard-coded fake matchup with two random decimal numbers. No sports, leagues, players, props, books or sharp-book prices. No live in-play odds and no scores.
result.price_and_free_tier: Free to read. The code needs only Python 3.9+, fastapi and uvicorn, which are free and open source. There is no data plan or free tier because there is no data vendor. The article mentions Firestore (optional) and Chart.js (optional), neither of which is an odds source. Read 2026-10-07.
result.terms_notes: I did not read Medium's terms of service. Medium's article and profile pages answered this container with a Cloudflare challenge (403, title "Attention Required! | Cloudflare"). I did not try to get past it, and I did not use paywall-bypass mirrors. Only the public RSS feed was read, one GET. The tutorial contains no scraping, so scraping clauses do not apply. It carries no data licence, because it has no data. No author repo or licence was found.

The prose says the loop 'sends JSON updates to all connected clients'. The code is a separate loop per connection with no connection manager or broadcast, so each client would see different random numbers.

verdict.why: This is not an odds or scores source. It is a toy WebSocket demo that streams random numbers every 3 seconds, with no vendor, no upstream and no timestamp. It is free only because it has no data, so it cannot beat CNO or the Novig makers. The technique is a FastAPI WebSocket relay that fans a feed out to browsers (Angular). Vigilant is a single-user Android app that can open the upstream sockets or REST polls itself (Polymarket, Sofascore and so on), so a relay would only add a hop, a host and latency. The tutorial's timer loop also decouples send time from change time, the opposite of what the bar needs. Even if a real feed were swapped in, a viewer would see that feed's age plus up to 3 s. Nothing here needs further research and nothing here needs a phone test. The real question is which upstream to relay, and this article does not answer it.
